match.reason: The bank point covers the adaptive immune response and the roles of B and T cells but never mentions lymph nodes, lymphatic trapping of antigens, or where the cells meet antigens, so it does not teach the new point's idea.

draft.title: The lymphatic system
card: The lymphatic system is a network of vessels and organs. Vessels carry lymph, a clear fluid that drains from tissues, and return it to the blood.
Lymph carries antigens from infected tissues to lymph nodes. Antigens are molecules that the immune system recognises as foreign.
Lymph nodes are small organs along the vessels. They trap antigens from the lymph, and many B cells and T cells wait inside them.
A B cell or T cell that has a receptor matching an antigen meets it in the node. This meeting starts the adaptive immune response.
draft.remember: Lymph carries antigens to the nodes, where B and T cells meet them.

a.q: Why are lymph nodes important for starting an adaptive immune response?
opts: They trap antigens where B and T cells can meet them
They make antigens that train B and T cells
They carry blood to infected tissues to destroy antigens
They store antibodies until an infection occurs
a.why: Lymph carries antigens into the nodes, which trap them. Many B and T cells are inside, so a cell with a matching receptor can meet its antigen. Nodes do not make antigens, which come from pathogens or foreign material.
a.clue: Think about what meets what inside a node.

b.q: Leon cuts his foot and bacteria enter the tissue. Which path would carry the bacterial antigens to the cells that start the adaptive response?
opts: Lymph vessels carry them to lymph nodes in the leg
Blood vessels carry them straight to the skin
Lymph vessels carry them back to the cut
Lymph nodes send them out to the bacteria
b.why: Lymph drains from the tissue and carries antigens along lymph vessels to nearby nodes. There, B and T cells can meet them. Lymph moves away from the tissue, not back to the cut.
b.clue: Lymph drains from tissues towards the nodes.

a.best: They trap antigens where B and T cells can meet them

b.best: Lymph vessels carry them to lymph nodes in the leg

problems.detail: The card defines antigens as molecules 'recognised as foreign'. The VCE Study Design teaches self-antigens as well as non-self antigens, so this definition conflicts with that distinction. A better definition is a molecule that can trigger an immune response.

The card implies T cells meet antigens trapped from the lymph directly. T cells recognise antigen only when it is presented on MHC, usually by antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells that travel to the node. At Year 12 VCE level this could mislead students.
The clue 'Lymph drains from tissues towards the nodes' practically states the right option. It is the only option where lymph vessels carry antigens to nodes.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, but question b's clue gives the answer away. The card's antigen definition ('recognised as foreign') clashes with VCE self-antigens. The card also implies T cells meet free antigen without antigen presentation.

proposal.title: The lymphatic system
card: The lymphatic system is a network of vessels and organs. Vessels carry lymph, a clear fluid that drains from tissues, and return it to the blood.
Antigens are molecules that can trigger an immune response. Lymph carries free antigens, and dendritic cells that have taken up antigens, from infected tissues to lymph nodes.
Lymph nodes are small organs along the vessels. They trap antigens from the lymph, and many B cells and T cells wait inside them.

A B cell can bind a matching antigen directly. A T cell recognises an antigen only when an antigen-presenting cell, such as a dendritic cell, shows it on MHC markers (proteins on the cell surface). These meetings in the node start the adaptive response.
proposal.remember: Lymph brings antigens to the nodes. B cells can bind them directly, but T cells need them presented.

a.q: Why are lymph nodes important for starting an adaptive immune response?
opts: They trap antigens where B and T cells can meet them
They make antigens that train B and T cells
They carry blood to infected tissues to destroy antigens
They store antibodies until an infection occurs
a.why: Lymph brings antigens and dendritic cells into the nodes, where many B and T cells wait. A cell with a matching receptor can meet its antigen there. Nodes do not make antigens, which come from pathogens or other material.
a.clue: Think about what meets what inside a node.

b.q: Leon cuts his foot and bacteria enter it. How does a T cell in a lymph node in his leg first recognise a bacterial antigen?
opts: A dendritic cell presents the antigen to it on MHC
It binds free antigen that the node trapped from lymph
It leaves the node and binds the bacteria in the cut
It binds antigen carried to the node in the blood
b.why: A T cell recognises antigen only when it is shown on MHC by an antigen-presenting cell. Dendritic cells take up antigen in the foot and carry it to the node. Free antigen trapped in the node can be bound by B cells, but not by T cells.
b.clue: Can a T cell recognise an antigen on its own?

a.best: They trap antigens where B and T cells can meet them

b.best: A dendritic cell presents the antigen to it on MHC
